message.content:
In Texas, tenants have a number of statutory rights designed to protect them from unfair treatment and to ensure safe, habitable housing. Below is an overview of key rights you should know. (This is not legal advice; if you have a specific dispute, consult a qualified attorney.) | Category | Key Rights | What It Means | |----------|------------|---------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlord may charge up to one month’s rent for a furnished unit, two months for an unfurnished unit.
• Must be returned within 30 days after lease ends, minus deductions for damages beyond normal wear. | Landlords cannot keep deposits without proper documentation or exceed the statutory limit. | | **Habitability** | • Landlord must maintain plumbing, heating, electrical, structural integrity, and pest control.
• Must provide adequate water, heat, and sanitation. | If the unit is unsafe or uninhabitable, you can withhold rent or repair and deduct. | | **Repair and Deduct** | • If landlord fails to fix major problems, you may repair and deduct reasonable costs from rent. | Must keep receipts and notify landlord in writing. | | **Notice Requirements** | • For non‑payment of rent: 3‑day notice before eviction.
• For lease termination: 30‑day notice for month‑to‑month, 60‑day for longer leases.
• For entry: 24‑hour written notice unless emergency. | Landlords cannot enter without notice or evict without following procedure. | | **Eviction Process** | • Must file a lawsuit in district court.
• Court will issue a summons and order.
• Eviction can only occur after a judgment and sheriff’s execution. | Landlords cannot forcibly remove you or lock you out. | | **Discrimination** | • Protected under federal Fair Housing Act and Texas Property Code §92.001.
• No discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, family status, or source of income. | Landlords cannot refuse to rent or impose different terms because of protected characteristics. | | **Lease Terms** | • Landlord cannot add unreasonable restrictions (e.g., “no pets” if not stated).
• Must honor lease terms unless mutually agreed to change. | You can negotiate changes or refuse to comply with illegal clauses. | | **Rent Increases** | • No statutory cap on rent increases, but must give proper notice (usually 30 days). | Landlords cannot raise rent without notice or in violation of lease. | | **Right to Quiet Enjoyment** | • Landlord must not interfere with your peaceful use of the premises. | Excessive noise, harassment, or repeated entries violate this right. | | **Maintenance of Records** | • Landlord must keep records of rent payments and repairs. | You can request copies if needed. | | **Legal Remedies** | • Can sue for damages, recover unpaid rent, or seek injunctions.
• Can file complaints with the Texas Attorney General’s Office or local housing agencies. | Provides avenues for enforcement. | ### Practical Tips 1. **Document Everything** – Keep copies of lease, receipts, emails, and photos of any damage or maintenance issues. 2. **Written Notices** – Send all notices (repair requests, rent payment notices, entry notices) via certified mail or email with read receipt. 3. **Know Your Lease** – Read it thoroughly; many disputes arise from misunderstandings of lease clauses. 4. **Seek Mediation** – Before filing suit, consider mediation services offered by local courts or community organizations. 5. **Legal Aid** – If you cannot afford an attorney, look for nonprofit legal aid clinics in Texas that specialize in housing law. --- #### Quick Reference Checklist - [ ] Security deposit returned within 30 days (minus legitimate deductions). - [ ] Landlord maintains habitability standards. - [ ] Proper notice given for entry, rent increase, or lease termination. - [ ] No unlawful eviction or lockout. - [ ] No discrimination in renting or leasing terms. - [ ] Right to quiet enjoyment upheld. If you encounter a specific issue—such as a landlord refusing to return a deposit, failing to make repairs, or threatening eviction—consult a Texas attorney who specializes in landlord‑tenant law. They can help you enforce your rights and navigate the legal process.
